simple: the flight controller's best guess of how the vehicle is tilted and which way it points.
analogy: Amara's feeling of how level her tray is.
precise: an estimate of the rotation between the body frame and the world frame (here roll, pitch and yaw, or a quaternion), computed from sensor readings because no sensor measures the rotation itself.
source: B1 of F10-13 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); U1 of F10-13 (University chapters) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what an accelerometer really feels: every push on the vehicle except gravity, divided by its mass.
analogy: the pull Amara feels in her arms, which changes when she speeds up.
precise: f = a − gworld, the vehicle's acceleration minus the gravitational acceleration, expressed in the sensor's axes; at rest it equals +g pointing up, in free fall it is zero.
source: B1 of F10-13 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-13 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the small rate a gyro reports when it is not turning at all.
analogy: a wrist that always feels a faint twist that is not there.
precise: the slowly varying offset b in the gyro model ωmeasured = ω + b + noise; in this chapter's recording b = (0.004, −0.006, 0.003) rad/s, an exercise value.
source: B1 of F10-13 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); R1 of F10-13 (Lab run of record_flight.cpp) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an error that keeps growing because small mistakes are added up again and again.
analogy: the tray that creeps to a slant during a long walk.
precise: the error of an estimate obtained by integrating a rate; a constant bias b grows the error linearly as b t, and white noise grows it like a random walk.
source: D1 of F10-13 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); U1 of F10-13 (University chapters)

simple: roll and pitch worked out by assuming the accelerometer points at "up".
analogy: Amara judging level from the pull on her arms.
precise: roll = atan2(fy, fz), pitch = atan2(−fx, √(fy² + fz²)) in DN201's axes; correct only when the vehicle's acceleration is zero.
source: D1 of F10-13 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F10-13 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the sensor board sits slightly crooked on the frame.
analogy: a tray with one short leg on its stand.
precise: a fixed rotation between the IMU's axes and the vehicle's body axes; if it is not measured and removed, every estimate is off by it.
source: D1 of F10-13 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); U1 of F10-13 (University chapters)

simple: a way to mix two sensors so that each one is used where it is good.
analogy: trusting your wrists for quick tips and your sense of "down" for the long run.
precise: an estimator x̂ = H(s) x1 + (1 − H(s)) x2 whose two filters add up to one at every frequency; for attitude, a high-pass on the integrated gyro and a low-pass on the accelerometer tilt.
source: B1 of F10-14 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); B2 of F10-14 (Robert Mahony, Tarek Hamel, Jean-Michel Pflimlin, "Nonlinear Complementary Filters on the Special Orthogonal Group", IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 2008); D1 of F10-14 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a low-pass keeps slow changes and smooths fast ones away; a high-pass does the opposite.
analogy: the slow nudge toward "down" and the quick wrist reaction.
precise: first-order filters 1/(τs + 1) and τs/(τs + 1); below the corner frequency 1/τ rad/s the low-pass passes the signal, above it the high-pass does (MA301 F0-72).
source: U1 of F10-14 (University chapters); D1 of F10-14 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: how slow the nudge toward "down" is.
analogy: how many seconds Amara waits before her sense of "down" wins.
precise: the time constant shared by the two filters; at sample period dt the discrete weight on the gyro path is α = τ/(τ + dt).
source: D1 of F10-14 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs)

simple: a rule that ignores the accelerometer when its reading looks suspicious.
analogy: not trusting your sense of "down" while you are clearly braking.
precise: a test on the measurement (here |f| between 0.9 g and 1.1 g) that decides whether the accelerometer correction is applied to this sample.
source: D1 of F10-14 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F10-14 (Robert Mahony, Tarek Hamel, Jean-Michel Pflimlin, "Nonlinear Complementary Filters on the Special Orthogonal Group", IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 2008) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a slow memory that learns the gyro's constant error and subtracts it.
analogy: Amara noticing that her wrists always feel a faint twist to the left, and ignoring it.
precise: the ki term of the vector filter, b̂ ← b̂ − ki e dt, which removes a constant gyro bias from the attitude error at the cost of slower, coupled dynamics.
source: B2 of F10-14 (Robert Mahony, Tarek Hamel, Jean-Michel Pflimlin, "Nonlinear Complementary Filters on the Special Orthogonal Group", IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 2008); D1 of F10-14 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: working out attitude, speed and position mostly from the IMU, and correcting the result with satellite fixes.
analogy: Amara walking by feel, with a friend calling out her speed.
precise: a filter whose prediction integrates gyro rates into attitude and rotated specific force plus gravity into velocity and position, and whose updates use GNSS position and velocity; here an EKF with 12 states including the gyro bias.
source: B1 of F10-15 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-15 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: feeding the IMU readings into the prediction step instead of treating them as measurements.
analogy: counting your own steps to know where you are, instead of asking someone.
precise: the gyro and accelerometer enter the process model xk = f(xk−1, uk) as the input u; their noise appears in the process noise Q, and no model of the vehicle's forces or motor thrust is needed.
source: B1 of F10-15 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-15 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how surprising a measurement is, in units of how surprising it is allowed to be.
analogy: the friend's speed call compared with what Amara expected, judged by how sure both of them are.
precise: for innovation component yi with predicted variance Sii, the ratio |yi|/√Sii; in this chapter's code a ratio above the gate rejects the sample. Flight stacks define their own ratios (unverified box).
source: D1 of F10-15 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); U1 of F10-15 (University chapters)

simple: the limit above which a measurement is thrown away as nonsense.
analogy: ignoring the friend if he suddenly shouts that you are running at 40 km/h.
precise: a threshold on the test ratio (here 5) or on the normalised innovation squared; it protects the state from outliers, at the risk of rejecting good data after the state itself has gone wrong.
source: D1 of F10-15 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R3 of F10-15 (Lab run of checks.cpp, which recomputes the numbers in the text, the worked example and the answer key)

simple: whether the measurements carry any information about a state at all.
analogy: the friend's speed calls tell Amara about her push, but nothing about which way she faces while she stands still.
precise: a state is observable if different values of it produce different measurement histories; for the INS, yaw and the z-gyro bias are observable only while the vehicle accelerates horizontally.
source: D1 of F10-15 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F10-15 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: controllers stacked inside each other, where each one gives the next one its target.
analogy: manager → team leader → worker → hands.
precise: a nested arrangement of feedback loops in which the output of an outer controller is the setpoint of the inner one; for a multirotor: position → velocity → attitude → body rate → torque.
source: B1 of F10-16 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-16 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what a loop was asked to do, plotted next to what it achieved.
analogy: the order Amara was given next to what she did.
precise: the pair (reference, measured state) logged for each loop of a cascade; the loop whose actual value fails to follow its own setpoint is the one at fault.
source: D1 of F10-16 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R1 of F10-16 (Lab run of Listing 2 (loop_steps.cpp with cascade.hpp))

simple: each inner loop must be clearly faster than the loop around it.
analogy: the hands react many times before the worker changes the lean.
precise: the design rule that the closed-loop bandwidth of an inner loop is several times (often quoted as 3 to 10) that of the outer loop, so the outer loop can treat the inner one as nearly ideal.
source: B1 of F10-16 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice"); D1 of F10-16 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the direction and size of the push the rotors must give to produce the wanted acceleration.
analogy: how Amara must lean the tray to speed up without spilling.
precise: F = m (asp + g ez); its direction is the wanted body z axis, which together with the yaw setpoint fixes the attitude setpoint, and its component along the current body z axis is the thrust command.
source: D1 of F10-16 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F10-16 (Randal W. Beard, Timothy W. McLain, "Small Unmanned Aircraft: Theory and Practice") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the most the controller is allowed to lean the vehicle.
analogy: Amara never tips the tray more than a set angle, whatever the team leader asks.
precise: a bound on the angle between the thrust vector and the vertical (35° in this chapter's code), applied by scaling the horizontal acceleration setpoint to at most (g + az) tan(limit).
source: D1 of F10-16 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R3 of F10-16 (Lab run of checks.cpp, which recomputes the numbers in the text, the worked example and the answer key (W4, W5 and K1 use R1's rise times as printed constants))

simple: the innermost loop, which makes the vehicle spin at the speed it is asked for.
analogy: Amara's hands reacting to the tray starting to tip.
precise: a PID per body axis from rate error (setpoint minus gyro) to angular acceleration, multiplied by the inertia to give torque (Listing 1 of F10-16, lines 165–169); its output goes through the mixer to the motors.
source: D1 of F10-17 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); U1 of F10-17 (University chapters)

simple: how fast a loop reaches a new setpoint, and how far it goes past it.
analogy: how fast the hands level the tray, and whether they tip it the other way.
precise: rise time is the time from 10 % to 90 % of a step; overshoot is the peak above the step, in percent of the step.
source: D1 of F10-17 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); U1 of F10-17 (University chapters)

simple: a smoother on the derivative part, so that sensor noise does not reach the motors amplified.
analogy: Amara ignoring the floor's tiny tremors and reacting only to real tipping.
precise: a low-pass filter (here first-order, time constant 5 ms, corner 31.8 Hz) on the differentiated measurement; without it, white gyro noise of σ is amplified by about kd √2 σ/dt.
source: D1 of F10-17 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R3 of F10-17 (Lab run of checks.cpp, which recomputes the numbers in the text, the worked example and the answer key)

simple: how well the loop holds its setpoint when something pushes it.
analogy: keeping the tray level when one glass is heavier.
precise: the remaining rate error under a constant disturbance torque; a P-only loop leaves (disturbance angular acceleration)/kp, an integrator drives it to zero over a time of order (disturbance)/(ki × error).
source: D1 of F10-17 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R1 of F10-17 (Lab run of Listing 1 (rate_tune.cpp))

simple: running the real flight software on a computer, flying a simulated vehicle.
analogy: Amara practising the route with an empty tray in an empty café.
precise: the flight stack compiled for the host computer and connected to a physics simulator in place of sensors and motors, so its controllers, parameters and logs can be exercised without hardware.
source: D2 of F10-17 (PX4 project (Dronecode Foundation), PX4 Autopilot User Guide); D1 of F10-17 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rule that says what to give up first when the motors cannot do everything asked.
analogy: keep the tray level first, then its height, then turn it.
precise: an ordering of the wrench components (here roll and pitch torque, collective thrust, yaw torque) such that an allocator meets each component fully before the next, and reduces only the lowest-priority components when the rotor limits are reached.
source: D1 of F10-18 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); D2 of F10-18 (PX4 project (Dronecode Foundation), PX4 Autopilot User Guide: control allocation and airmode pages) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: raising or lowering all four motors together so that the differences between them fit.
analogy: lifting or lowering the whole hand so every fingertip can still press its share.
precise: adding the same force to all rotors (a change of collective thrust only) so that the torque-producing differences lie inside [0, fmax]; it trades thrust accuracy for torque accuracy.
source: D1 of F10-18 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R1 of F10-18 (Lab run of Listing 2 (allocation.cpp with allocation.hpp))

simple: how much turning torque the rotors can make, which is small for a quadcopter.
analogy: turning the tray by twisting fingertips: possible, but weak.
precise: the largest yaw torque available while other demands are met; it comes from the rotors' reaction torques (coefficient c = kQ/kT = 0.015 m for the course quad), giving 4 c fhover = 0.147 N·m at hover thrust if thrust is kept.
source: D1 of F10-18 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R3 of F10-18 (Lab run of checks.cpp, which recomputes the numbers in the text, the worked example and the answer key)

simple: when cutting each motor at its limit creates a push or a turn nobody asked for.
analogy: one fingertip that cannot press harder makes the tray tilt sideways.
precise: the error in the produced wrench, including non-zero components that were zero in the request, caused by clipping rotor commands independently after an exact inverse mixer.
source: D1 of F10-18 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R1 of F10-18 (Lab run of Listing 2 (allocation.cpp with allocation.hpp))

simple: the gain at which a loop stops calming down after a kick and keeps swinging.
analogy: how hard the waiter's hands can react before the tray starts to buzz on its own.
precise: the smallest proportional gain at which the closed loop no longer returns to rest after a disturbance; the oscillation frequency there is the ultimate frequency. The gain margin of a tuning is Ku divided by its gain (MA301 F0-72).
source: D1 of F10-19 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); U1 of F10-19 (University chapters)

simple: the time between something happening to the vehicle and the controller's answer reaching the motors.
analogy: how late the waiter's hands react.
precise: the sum of sensing, filtering, computation and actuation delays in a loop; a delay T adds a phase lag of 360° × f × T at frequency f without changing the gain, which lowers the ultimate gain.
source: D1 of F10-19 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R2 of F10-19 (Lab run of Listing 2 (margins.cpp))

simple: a swing that dies out only slowly, so any noise keeps it going.
analogy: the tray that keeps buzzing because the floor keeps trembling.
precise: the response of a stable loop with closed-loop poles close to the imaginary axis; with noise or repeated inputs it looks like a sustained oscillation at the loop's resonance, without the loop being unstable.
source: D1 of F10-19 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R1 of F10-19 (Lab run of the forensic evidence program osc_log.cpp (Listing 1))

simple: not letting the controllers' memories build up while the vehicle sits on the ground.
analogy: Amara not pressing against the counter while the tray rests on it.
precise: a rule that keeps the integrators of the attitude-related loops at zero (or frozen) while a landed detector reports ground contact, and releases them only after lift-off.
source: D1 of F10-19 (derivations shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R3 of F10-19 (Lab run of Listing 3 (windup.cpp))
